opus-5.5.text:
I think it's actually a much more interesting process than we usually give it credit for. Most of the time we don't just "look" and then read off an answer. Perception is active and driven by the question.

Say I ask you, "Where did I leave my keys?" You don't process every pixel of the room with equal weight. You start with a hypothesis, maybe "probably on the table by the door." That hypothesis guides where your eyes go. You glance there, and if they're not there you update and look somewhere else. So there's a loop between reasoning and seeing. The question shapes the looking, and the looking reshapes your reasoning.

A few things stand out to me about this.

First, it's very spatial. You have a mental model of the room: where things are, how far apart, what's behind what. You're not working with a flat image. You're working with a 3D, persistent representation of the world, and you carry it with you even when you're not looking at it.

Second, it's selective. Humans are very good at deciding what to ignore. Attention isn't a side feature. It's what makes it possible to answer questions efficiently in a cluttered visual world.

Third, a lot of it happens before language. When you look for your keys you're not narrating "now I'm checking the table" to yourself. Much of the reasoning is visual. Language comes in when you need to explain it, but it's not necessarily the substrate of the thinking.

That's partly why I think the current way many multimodal models work is a bit unnatural. Typically you encode the image once, pass it to a language model, and then do all the reasoning in text. It's like glancing at a scene for half a second, closing your eyes, and trying to answer everything from memory using words. Humans don't do that. We go back and look again, we zoom in, we move around, we use spatial memory.

So when I think about building visual intelligence, the question for me isn't only "can the model recognize objects?" It's whether the model can see in a question-driven, iterative, spatially grounded way. Can it decide where to look, keep a model of the world in its head, and reason visually rather than just translating everything into language? I think that's where a lot of the important open problems are.

r001.rationale: The response says a question guides where someone looks and illustrates searching for keys, but it does not explain that a person asked an object's color first tries to locate that object.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that most of the time, people don't "arrive" at an answer at all, not in the deliberate sense. If you ask me what's on the table in front of me, I don't reason toward it. I just see it. The perception is the answer. That's the fast path, and it covers the vast majority of what we do visually.

But then there's a second kind of question, and this is the kind I find much more interesting. If you ask me how many chairs are in this room, or whether that cup would fit on that shelf, or what's behind the person sitting next to you, I can't just read it off the image. I have to do something. I move my eyes around. I count. I mentally rotate things. I build a little model in my head of where things are relative to each other, and then I query that model. The answer comes from the process, not from the glance.

That distinction matters a lot to me because it's exactly where current multimodal models fall apart. They are extremely good at the first kind, the recognition kind, because that's what language supervision gives you. You see a picture, you describe it, you've matched the words. But the second kind, where you need spatial reasoning, where you need to remember what you saw three seconds ago in a video and relate it to what you see now, the models are shockingly weak. They'll tell you there are five chairs when there are two, and they'll say it confidently.

And I think the reason is that humans have this thing we might call a cognitive map. When I walk through a space, I'm building an internal representation of it that persists even after the visual input is gone. I can close my eyes and tell you where the door is. Language models don't naturally build that. They process the frames, they produce tokens, but there's no persistent spatial structure in between. So part of what we're trying to figure out in our research is whether you can get models to form that kind of representation, and what it would even look like inside a transformer.

So to come back to your question, I'd say humans arrive at visual answers in two very different ways, and we've mostly only solved one of them.

r001.rationale: The response describes recognizing what is on a table and using deliberate processes for other visual questions, but it does not say that a person first locates an object when asked about its color.

astra-6.text:
I think it starts with the question directing our attention. We don’t necessarily process every detail in a scene equally. If you ask me what’s on the table, I’ll look toward the table, identify the objects there, and connect what I see with concepts I already know. Then I can express an answer in language.

So even though it feels almost instantaneous, there’s an interaction between perception, attention, memory, and reasoning. And it can be iterative: if I’m uncertain, I might look again or shift my viewpoint. We’re actively gathering the visual information we need to answer the question.

r001.rationale: The response says a question directs attention and gives an example of looking toward a table to identify objects, but it does not explain that when asked for an object's color, a person first locates that object.

sol-6.1.text: I think it’s an interaction between perception and reasoning. You look at the scene, identify the things that might matter to the question, and connect what you see with what you already know. And it’s not necessarily a single pass. You might form a hypothesis, look again at a particular part of the scene, and revise your answer. So the question itself helps guide your attention—what you look at and what information you need to extract.

r001.rationale: The response says people identify relevant things and use the question to guide attention, but it does not clearly state that they first locate the object whose color is being asked about.
